strengths: The orientation-resolved analysis reveals structured successes and failures that average accuracy conceals. These findings have an identifiable audience in out-of-distribution robustness, representation learning, and computational neuroscience.

The experimental coverage is substantial: three object categories, several seed orientation ranges, varying proportions of fully-seen instances, and multiple architectures. Five repetitions and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and reduced training data strengthen the descriptive findings.

The fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm and main heatmaps communicate the experimental question clearly. The geometric model offers an interpretable description of generalization patterns, and the manuscript provides code and data links.
weaknesses: Necessary change: The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Sections 3.3–4 infer that invariance disseminates through shared features and drives generalization, but Figure 5 establishes associations between aggregate activation statistics and accuracy. Common image geometry or jointly learned representations could produce these associations without the proposed directional transfer. Either provide a targeted intervention or transfer control, or consistently present dissemination as a hypothesis. The conclusion that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs also needs qualification.

Necessary change: The invariance metric does not establish the claimed orientation-invariant coding. Equation 5 averages responses over orientations before Equation 6 compares them; strongly orientation-selective responses can have identical regional means and receive maximal invariance. The 95th-percentile activity filter does not resolve this problem and selects different contributing neuron–instance pairs across conditions. Validate the interpretation with orientation-resolved measurements and report sensitivity to the filter, or narrow the interpretation to similarity of mean activation.

Necessary clarification: The generalizable/non-generalizable partition depends on an insufficiently specified score scale. Section 2.5 thresholds the fitted model at 10% of its maximum, although Pearson-correlation fitting does not calibrate its offset or accuracy interpretation. Figure S9c displays scores around 1.8–2.4; applying the stated rule on that scale would classify every displayed orientation as generalizable. State any normalization or distinction between the plotted and thresholded scores, and establish threshold robustness before relying on this partition in the neural analyses.

Necessary qualification: Section 2.4 optimizes the model using Pearson correlation, and Figures 4b/S5 report that same criterion without describing a held-out evaluation. The high correlations support a compact descriptive fit, but do not establish prediction on unseen orientations or experimental conditions. Clarify the fitting/evaluation separation and provide appropriate held-out evidence, or narrow the predictive claims.

Optional improvement: Report numerical correlations and uncertainty separately by architecture, seed, and orientation group alongside the pooled scatterplots. This would help readers distinguish relationships within conditions from differences between conditions.
